cards.title: NP versus P/poly
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\)? More explicitly, does there exist one language \(L\in\mathrm{NP}\) such that \[\forall C,k,N\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}\ \exists n\geq N:\quad\operatorname{CC}(L_n)>C(n+1)^k,\] where \(n\) is an integer, \(L_n\) is the characteristic function of \(L\) on \(n\)-bit strings and \(\operatorname{CC}\) is minimum Boolean circuit size in the model below?
cards.definitions:
A language is a subset \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), including the possible empty string. For each integer \(n\geq0\), its characteristic function \(L_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) is 1 exactly on strings in \(L\). An \(n\)-input Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with designated input nodes \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), optional constant nodes 0 and 1, binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output node. Gate inputs are edges from earlier nodes in a topological order; two inputs to a gate may be the same node. A node may feed arbitrarily many later gates. There is no depth restriction. Size is the number of AND, OR and NOT gates; input and constant nodes and output designation cost no gates. In particular a constant function has size zero. Every gate is evaluated in the ordinary Boolean way, and the output must equal \(L_n\) on every input, without error. Define \(\operatorname{CC}(L_n)\) as the minimum circuit size; a finite circuit always exists, for example from the truth table.

A circuit family is one circuit \(B_n\) for each length \(n\). It is nonuniform: there need not be a computable procedure mapping \(n\) to \(B_n\). The chosen circuit may depend on the length and on \(L\), but not on the particular input string of that length. The class \(\mathrm{P/poly}\) consists of languages for which there exist integers \(C,k\geq1\) and such a family computing \(L_n\) with at most \(C(n+1)^k\) gates for every \(n\geq0\). These constants may depend on \(L\), but not on \(n\).

For \(\mathrm{NP}\), require one deterministic multitape Turing-machine verifier \(V\), with a fixed finite program and tape alphabet and no advice or oracle, and integers \(a,b,D,d\geq1\), such that for every binary string \(x\), \[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists y\in\{0,1\}^*,\ |y|\leq a(|x|+1)^b:\ V(x,y)=1.\] On every pair of binary strings \((x,y)\), the verifier halts with one output bit within \(D(|x|+|y|+1)^d\) transitions. One explicit pair encoding is \(1^{|x|}0xy\), with the remainder after the indicated \(x\) interpreted as \(y\); malformed encodings are rejected in polynomial time. Each transition costs one step, including all bit arithmetic and input processing. The same verifier and constants work for every input of this one language.

The language \(L\) is chosen before the universal quantifiers over circuit bounds. It cannot change with \(k\), \(C\) or \(N\). Exceeding each bound at arbitrarily large lengths suffices; the conjecture does not demand exceeding it at every sufficiently large length. Conversely, if a polynomial bound holds except at finitely many lengths, enlarging its constant covers those lengths too, so this formulation is exactly noncontainment in \(\mathrm{P/poly}\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the noncontainment proposition or of its negation \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\). A separation must supply one NP language that escapes every polynomial circuit-size bound with the quantifier order stated above. Different languages for different exponents are insufficient. To establish containment, prove that every NP language has a polynomial-size nonuniform family; equivalently, polynomial-size circuits for one NP-complete language such as SAT at all input lengths suffice. No efficient or computable circuit generator is required. Lower bounds for circuits with extra depth or gate restrictions, or for a language only known to lie in a larger class than NP, do not alone settle the target.
cards.why: This is the central unrestricted Boolean circuit lower-bound question for efficiently verifiable languages. It asks whether NP remains hard even when a separate circuit can be chosen for each input length without an effective construction rule. A separation would strengthen Boolean P versus NP and illuminate the limits of nonuniform computation, with connections to the polynomial hierarchy, pseudorandomness and learning.

importance.reason: A foundational strengthening of P≠NP and the central target of general Boolean circuit lower bounds. Its consequences and methods reach across complexity, derandomization, learning, and cryptography.

progress.text: The Karp–Lipton theorem establishes \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\Rightarrow\mathrm{PH}=\Sigma_2^{\mathrm P}\); Wigderson’s Theorem 5.5 records the precise consequence.

Razborov and Rudich’s journal paper formalizes the natural-proofs barrier under a strong cryptographic hardness assumption. It constrains the specified properties, not all proofs of circuit lower bounds.

Williams proves that NEXP has no polynomial-size nonuniform ACC family, first at CCC 2011 and then in JACM 2014. This leaves both the NP language restriction and unrestricted gate-depth target unaddressed.

Chen, Tal and Wang’s ECCC paper gives \(n^{2.5-\varepsilon}\) lower bounds for depth-two threshold circuits and hard functions in \(\mathrm E^{\mathrm{NP}}\), for each fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\). It explicitly names NP versus P/poly as the broader open problem.

references.authors: Lijie Chen; Avishay Tal; Yichuan Wang
references.locator: ECCC TR26-039 submitted 14 March, published 15 March 2026. Full §1 and Theorem 1.1: for each epsilon in (0,1), an E^NP function lacks n^(2.5-epsilon)-size THR∘THR circuits. No newer revision shown on the checked report page.

cards.status_note: Explicitly posed by Wigderson and retained as the flagship circuit problem in Chen–Tal–Wang’s March 2026 introduction. A bounded primary-source check through 14 September 2026 located no unconditional resolution of NP versus unrestricted polynomial-size circuits. The checked ACC, threshold and natural-proofs results have different language classes, circuit restrictions or hypotheses; this review does not independently verify every cited proof.

context_blocks.text: Unrolling a polynomial-time computation gives polynomial-size circuits, so \(\mathrm P\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\). The reverse containment fails: a language whose membership depends only on length can be represented by one constant circuit per length even if the sequence of membership bits is undecidable. Thus \(\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\) implies \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\); a uniform P versus NP separation alone does not establish the circuit claim.

Counting shows that most Boolean truth tables need exponentially large circuits. It does not identify one language in NP: choosing a hard truth table independently at each length need not give polynomially verifiable membership. This explains the requirement that one fixed NP language escape every polynomial bound.

By the Karp–Lipton theorem, the opposite outcome \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\) would imply \(\mathrm{PH}=\Sigma_2^{\mathrm P}\), collapsing the polynomial hierarchy to its second level. That consequence is not a known contradiction: strictness of the hierarchy is itself unresolved.

SAT asks whether a finite Boolean formula has a satisfying assignment. Its NP-completeness and closure of polynomial-size circuit computation under polynomial-time reductions make polynomial-size circuits for SAT equivalent to \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\). An ordinary explicit formula encoding is sufficient for this equivalence; the main statement uses languages directly and imposes no encoding-dependent exponential lower-bound target.

The natural-proofs barrier is conditional on the strong cryptographic hardness premise in Razborov and Rudich’s theorem. Roughly, a property of \(n\)-variable truth tables cannot simultaneously be recognizable in time polynomial in the \(2^n\)-bit table, hold for a sufficiently large fraction of tables and be useful against polynomial-size circuits under that premise. The running-time scale is the full truth table. This limits a specified class of properties, rather than every mathematical proof.

Williams proves \(\mathrm{NEXP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{ACC}\), where NEXP allows nondeterministic time \(2^{n^{O(1)}}\), and ACC families have fixed depth and a fixed modulus \(m>1\), with unbounded-fan-in AND, OR and modular-counting gates and NOT gates. A modular gate tests whether the number of 1 inputs is divisible by \(m\). Both the allowed language class and the restricted circuit class differ from this card’s target.

Chen, Tal and Wang’s March 2026 Theorem 1.1 gives, for every fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), a function in \(\mathrm E^{\mathrm{NP}}\) without \(n^{2.5-\varepsilon}\)-size depth-two threshold circuits. Here \(\mathrm E^{\mathrm{NP}}\) means deterministic time \(2^{O(n)}\) with an NP oracle; a threshold gate tests whether a weighted sum of its Boolean inputs reaches a threshold. The function is not asserted to be in NP, the circuits have depth two and the bound has a fixed polynomial exponent. The paper explicitly retains NP versus P/poly as the broader open target.

cards.title: Planted clique conjecture
cards.formal: Is the following hardness statement true? For every fixed real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), with \(k_n=\lfloor n^{1/2-\varepsilon}\rfloor\), there is no uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) for which \[\Pr[\widehat b=b]\geq\frac23\] in the balanced one-graph experiment below for every sufficiently large integer \(n\).
cards.definitions:
For \(n\geq2\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The null distribution \(N_n\) is the distribution of a simple undirected labeled graph on \([n]\) in which each unordered pair of distinct vertices is an edge independently with probability \(1/2\). For \(0\leq k\leq n\), the planted distribution \(P_{n,k}\) chooses \(S\) uniformly among all \(k\)-element subsets of \([n]\), includes every edge inside \(S\), and chooses each other edge independently with probability \(1/2\). There are no loops. The planted set has exactly \(k\) vertices; it is not formed by independently including each vertex.

In the experiment, first choose a fair bit \(b\). If \(b=0\), sample \(G\sim N_n\); if \(b=1\), sample \(G\sim P_{n,k_n}\). Give \(A\) only \((n,k_n,G)\), and let \(\widehat b\in\{0,1\}\) be its output. All randomness of the sampling and of \(A\) is independent. Success is averaged over \(b\), the graph, the planted set when present and the algorithm’s random bits. Writing \(s_A(n,\varepsilon)\) for this probability, \[s_A(n,\varepsilon)=\tfrac12\big(\Pr_{G\sim N_n,A}[A(n,k_n,G)=0]+\Pr_{G\sim P_{n,k_n},A}[A(n,k_n,G)=1]\big).\] This is not a separate \(2/3\) guarantee on each individual graph or on each of the two distributions. The algorithm receives one sampled graph, without the label \(b\), the set \(S\), sample access to the unknown distribution or other side information.

For \(u\geq0\), define \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^a0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(a\) bits and no leading zeroes. The input is \(1^n0\operatorname{code}(k)\), followed by the full \(n^2\) adjacency matrix in row order, with no trailing bits. A valid input has \(n\geq2\), \(0\leq k\leq n\), a symmetric matrix and zero diagonal; let \(L\) be its full bit length. An allowed algorithm is one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and tape alphabet, using fresh independent fair bits and no oracle or advice. For some integers \(C,c\geq1\), on every input and every random-bit sequence it outputs one bit within \(C(L+1)^c\) transitions. Malformed encodings return 0 within this bound. Input processing, bit arithmetic and any additional graphs generated by the algorithm count toward time. On valid inputs \(L=\Theta(n^2)\), so polynomial time in \(L\) and in \(n\) are equivalent.

For each fixed \(\varepsilon\), the forbidden guarantee is \(\exists A,C,c,N\ \forall n\geq N:\ s_A(n,\varepsilon)\geq2/3\), with the global clock condition just specified. The program and constants may depend on this fixed \(\varepsilon\), but cannot change with \(n\); \(\varepsilon\) is not supplied as an oracle or an infinite advice string. The supplied integer \(k_n\) removes any need to compute a real power to construct the input. The conjecture therefore says that every allowed algorithm has success below \(2/3\) for arbitrarily large \(n\), for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). It does not assert that its success tends to \(1/2\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of this hardness proposition or its logical negation. To refute it, give some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), one allowed polynomial-time algorithm and a proof that its balanced success is at least \(2/3\) for every sufficiently large \(n\). To prove it, exclude every such algorithm for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). Success only on infinitely many sizes does not satisfy the refutation target. A limitation on sum-of-squares relaxations, local searches or another restricted model does not establish hardness against all allowed machines. A recovery result must imply the stated detection guarantee; a change of planting distribution or a conditional theorem must not be treated as an unconditional resolution of this exact experiment.
cards.why: A foundational average-case hardness hypothesis, planted clique isolates a gap between statistical information and efficient computation. The hidden clique is far larger than cliques arising by chance, yet no unrestricted polynomial-time detector is established in this regime. Related assumptions support hardness results for estimation, clustering and other inference tasks. Proving this formulation would imply Boolean \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\): a polynomial-time general clique decider would distinguish these distributions once \(k_n\) exceeds the typical null clique size.

importance.reason: A canonical computational threshold with broad consequences in average-case complexity, statistical inference, and the study of algorithmic lower-bound frameworks.

progress.text: Alon, Krivelevich and Sudakov obtain polynomial-time recovery for every fixed positive constant times \(\sqrt n\), with a polynomial exponent that can depend on that constant.
The nearly tight sum-of-squares integrality gap first appears in 2016 and is published in SIAM Journal on Computing in 2019. It limits the specified relaxation, rather than all detection algorithms.
The final gradient-descent preprint proves recovery at a sufficiently large constant times \(\sqrt n\) from full-graph initialization, for each fixed desired error probability.
Nagda and Raghavendra’s revised paper derives optimal efficient distinguishing advantages under a hypothesis in the independent-vertex planting model.
COLT 2026 presents robust algorithms for overlapping cliques in random intersection graphs above the stated \(\sqrt{n\log n}\) scale. This is a different distribution.

A new preprint reports conditional average-case hardness for Betti-number estimation from fixed-size planted-clique detection, with a separate quantum hypothesis. This review did not independently verify its reduction.

cards.status_note: No unconditional proof or unrestricted polynomial-time refutation of this exact fixed-size, balanced constant-success hypothesis was located in a bounded check through 14 September 2026. The cited sum-of-squares theorem is a relaxation/refutation lower bound; the optimal-advantage and September 2026 topology results are conditional, and several newer recovery results use other random graph models. Source/model review does not independently certify every cited proof.

context_blocks.text: The original provenance paper discusses statistical–computational gaps and proves lower bounds for low-degree polynomial procedures in latent models. The card retains the concrete fixed-size, balanced constant-success detection question already selected here. Those choices specify one version of the planted-clique hypothesis; they are not an unrestricted hardness theorem of the provenance paper.

There is enough information to distinguish the distributions. For \(r=\lceil3\log_2 n\rceil\), a union bound gives \(\Pr_{N_n}[\text{an }r\text{-clique exists}]\leq n^r2^{-r(r-1)/2}\to0\), while the planted graph contains such a clique for all sufficiently large \(n\), since \(k_n\geq r\). Thus exhaustive testing of all \(r\)-subsets gives success tending to one in \(n^{O(\log n)}\) time. The unresolved requirement is polynomial time.

Alon, Krivelevich and Sudakov give polynomial-time recovery of the hidden clique at every fixed positive constant times \(\sqrt n\), with success tending to one. Checking the reported clique gives detection as well. The polynomial exponent may depend on that constant; substituting the vanishing quantity \(n^{-\varepsilon}\) for it does not produce a fixed polynomial bound below the square-root scale.

Barak and coauthors show that degree-\(d\) sum-of-squares relaxations on a null random graph assign clique value \(n^{1/2-o(1)}\) when \(d=o(\log n)\), despite actual cliques being logarithmic in size. Their Remark 1.2 explicitly separates search, refutation and detection. The integrality gap rules out certain certificates of absence of a large clique; it is not an unrestricted lower bound for the balanced detector defined here.

Gheissari, Jagannath and Xu prove recovery by discrete gradient descent initialized at the full vertex set for \(k\geq C\sqrt n\), where \(C\) depends on the desired fixed error probability and the penalty parameter. Their Theorem 1.1 also analyzes a low-temperature chain. The theorem operates at the square-root scale and allows intermediate vertex sets that are not cliques.

Nagda and Raghavendra derive sharp efficient distinguishing advantages conditionally on a planted-clique hypothesis. Their model plants each vertex independently with probability \(k/n\), so clique size fluctuates; their advantage convention and eventual hardness hypothesis also differ from the exact guarantee here. The result strengthens consequences of its assumed hypothesis, without proving this card’s fixed-size hardness assertion.

Göbel, Ruff and Schiller’s COLT 2026 work concerns multiple overlapping planted cliques in random intersection graphs, with robust recovery for \(k\gg\sqrt{n\log n}\). Both its random graph distribution and signal regime differ from this single fixed-size planted-clique experiment.

A preprint posted on 11 September 2026 by Strelchuk, Subramanian and Wesołowski reports average-case hardness for Betti-number estimation through a planted-clique reduction. Its §3.2 uses a uniformly chosen planted set of fixed size. The reported hardness is conditional on a planted-clique conjecture, with a separate hypothesis for quantum algorithms; this review has not independently verified the new reduction.

cards.context:
The original provenance paper discusses statistical–computational gaps and proves lower bounds for low-degree polynomial procedures in latent models. The card retains the concrete fixed-size, balanced constant-success detection question already selected here. Those choices specify one version of the planted-clique hypothesis; they are not an unrestricted hardness theorem of the provenance paper.

There is enough information to distinguish the distributions. For \(r=\lceil3\log_2 n\rceil\), a union bound gives \(\Pr_{N_n}[\text{an }r\text{-clique exists}]\leq n^r2^{-r(r-1)/2}\to0\), while the planted graph contains such a clique for all sufficiently large \(n\), since \(k_n\geq r\). Thus exhaustive testing of all \(r\)-subsets gives success tending to one in \(n^{O(\log n)}\) time. The unresolved requirement is polynomial time.

Alon, Krivelevich and Sudakov give polynomial-time recovery of the hidden clique at every fixed positive constant times \(\sqrt n\), with success tending to one. Checking the reported clique gives detection as well. The polynomial exponent may depend on that constant; substituting the vanishing quantity \(n^{-\varepsilon}\) for it does not produce a fixed polynomial bound below the square-root scale.

Barak and coauthors show that degree-\(d\) sum-of-squares relaxations on a null random graph assign clique value \(n^{1/2-o(1)}\) when \(d=o(\log n)\), despite actual cliques being logarithmic in size. Their Remark 1.2 explicitly separates search, refutation and detection. The integrality gap rules out certain certificates of absence of a large clique; it is not an unrestricted lower bound for the balanced detector defined here.

Gheissari, Jagannath and Xu prove recovery by discrete gradient descent initialized at the full vertex set for \(k\geq C\sqrt n\), where \(C\) depends on the desired fixed error probability and the penalty parameter. Their Theorem 1.1 also analyzes a low-temperature chain. The theorem operates at the square-root scale and allows intermediate vertex sets that are not cliques.

Nagda and Raghavendra derive sharp efficient distinguishing advantages conditionally on a planted-clique hypothesis. Their model plants each vertex independently with probability \(k/n\), so clique size fluctuates; their advantage convention and eventual hardness hypothesis also differ from the exact guarantee here. The result strengthens consequences of its assumed hypothesis, without proving this card’s fixed-size hardness assertion.

Göbel, Ruff and Schiller’s COLT 2026 work concerns multiple overlapping planted cliques in random intersection graphs, with robust recovery for \(k\gg\sqrt{n\log n}\). Both its random graph distribution and signal regime differ from this single fixed-size planted-clique experiment.

A preprint posted on 11 September 2026 by Strelchuk, Subramanian and Wesołowski reports average-case hardness for Betti-number estimation through a planted-clique reduction. Its §3.2 uses a uniformly chosen planted set of fixed size. The reported hardness is conditional on a planted-clique conjecture, with a separate hypothesis for quantum algorithms; this review has not independently verified the new reduction.

cards.title: Hadwiger’s conjecture
cards.formal: Is the following proposition true? For every integer \(n\ge1\), every simple undirected graph \(G\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and every integer \(t\ge1\), if \(\chi(G)\ge t\), then \(G\) contains \(K_t\) as an ordinary graph minor. Equivalently, \(h(G)\ge\chi(G)\) for every such graph, where \(h\) is the Hadwiger number defined below.
cards.definitions: The edge set of \(G\) is any set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices in \([n]\); there are no loops or parallel edges. For an integer \(r\ge1\), a proper \(r\)-coloring is a map \(c:[n]\to\{1,\ldots,r\}\) such that \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). The chromatic number \(\chi(G)\) is the least such \(r\); it exists and lies between \(1\) and \(n\). The graph \(K_t\) has \(t\) vertices and every possible edge. A \(K_t\) minor in \(G\) means that there are \(t\) pairwise disjoint nonempty vertex sets \(B_1,\ldots,B_t\) with both of the following properties: for every \(i\), any two vertices of \(B_i\) are joined by a finite path of edges of \(G\) whose vertices all lie in \(B_i\); and for every \(i<j\), some edge of \(G\) has one endpoint in \(B_i\) and one in \(B_j\). A singleton is connected. The branch sets may have any sizes, need not cover all vertices, and have no restrictions on extra internal edges or on parity. This is equivalent to obtaining \(K_t\) by vertex deletions, edge deletions and edge contractions, discarding loops and merging parallel edges after contraction. It is neither an induced-minor nor an odd-minor requirement. The Hadwiger number \(h(G)\) is the largest \(t\) admitting these branch sets, so \(1\le h(G)\le n\). For \(t\ge2\), the proposition equivalently says that absence of a \(K_t\) minor implies a proper \((t-1)\)-coloring; the \(t=1\) assertion holds automatically for a nonempty graph. Relabeling vertices has no effect. The quantifiers impose no connectedness, degree, order or other restriction on \(G\), and no running-time bound on finding a coloring or a minor.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition for all finite nonempty simple undirected graphs and all integers \(t\ge1\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: existence of a finite graph \(G\) and integer \(t\ge1\) with \(\chi(G)\ge t\) and no \(t\) branch sets satisfying the definition. A counterexample must certify both the chromatic lower bound and absence of the ordinary clique minor. A proof of \(h(G)\ge\chi(G)\) for every graph is an equivalent positive answer. No efficient algorithm is required. A constant-factor or asymptotic coloring bound, a finite list of established values of \(t\), a restricted graph class, or a counterexample only to the odd-minor variant does not cover the target.
cards.why: Hadwiger’s conjecture proposes an exact relation between two basic graph parameters: the number of colors needed and the size of a complete graph obtainable by contraction. It extends the Four-Color Theorem and would turn exclusion of a complete minor into the sharp universal coloring bound. Its significance comes from this structural connection across all finite graphs, rather than from an algorithmic requirement in the question.

importance.reason: One of the central graph-theoretic conjectures, with an exact extremal target and consequences across coloring and minor structure.

context_blocks.text: A complete minor can be much larger than any complete subgraph: contraction groups connected regions into single vertices. Hadwiger asks whether the resulting complete graph can always have as many vertices as the original graph needs colors. For every \(t\ge2\), the graph \(K_{t-1}\) has no \(K_t\) minor and needs exactly \(t-1\) colors, so the conjectured bound for the excluded-minor class is sharp.

The exact cases through \(t=6\) are known. The \(t=5\) case is equivalent, via Wagner’s theorem, to the Four-Color Theorem for planar graphs. Robertson, Seymour and Thomas established the \(t=6\) case: without assuming four-colorability, their structural result makes a minimal counterexample apex, meaning that deleting one vertex leaves a planar graph. The Four-Color Theorem then gives five colors for that graph. Their paper indexes the conjecture by the allowed number of colors, one less than the clique-minor order used on this card.

Kostochka and Thomason obtained an \(O(t\sqrt{\log t})\) bound on degeneracy, where a graph is \(d\)-degenerate if every nonempty subgraph has a vertex of degree at most \(d\). Such a graph is \((d+1)\)-colorable. The order of this degeneracy bound is tight, but that fact is not a chromatic lower bound of the same order and does not disprove Hadwiger. Delcourt and Postle’s Theorem 1.5 gives \(O(t\log\log t)\) colors for arbitrary \(K_t\)-minor-free graphs; its quantification has no bound on the number of vertices.

Liu and Luo’s version 2, submitted on 9 September 2026, states in Theorem 1.1 that an absolute constant \(C\) satisfies \(\chi(G)\le Ct\log\log\log t\) for every integer \(t\ge16\) and every \(K_t\)-minor-free graph. Their logarithms are natural. This is recorded as a recent preprint claim whose proof has not been independently verified here. It does not establish either the weakening \(\chi(G)=O(t)\) or the exact bound \(t-1\); the introduction still identifies clique-minor orders starting at seven as open.

For the odd-minor variant, the disjoint branch trees must each have a proper two-coloring, with an edge joining vertices of the same color between every pair of trees. Forgetting these extra requirements yields an ordinary minor, so absence of an ordinary minor implies absence of an odd minor; the reverse implication need not hold. Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner and Wigderson’s December 2025 preprint states that for each fixed \(\delta>0\) and every sufficiently large \(t\), some graph has no odd \(K_t\) minor and has \(\chi(G)\ge(3/2-\delta)t\). This refutes the stronger odd-minor conjecture. Odd-minor absence by itself does not certify the ordinary-minor absence required for a negative answer here.

cards.title: Shub–Smale \(\tau\)-conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist an integer \(C\geq1\), independent of the polynomial, such that every nonzero \(f\in\mathbb Z[x]\) satisfies \[z_{\mathbb Z}(f)\leq(1+\tau(f))^C,\] where \(z_{\mathbb Z}(f)\) is the number of distinct integer roots and \(\tau(f)\) is the minimum number of additions, subtractions and multiplications needed to construct \(f\) from only \(1\) and \(x\)?
cards.definitions:
The ring \(\mathbb Z[x]\) consists of formal univariate polynomials with integer coefficients. A straight-line program of length \(s\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) starts with registers \(g_0=1\) and \(g_1=x\). For each \(i=2,\ldots,s+1\), it chooses \(j_i,k_i<i\) and one operation from \(\{+,-,\times\}\), and sets \(g_i=g_{j_i}\mathbin{\circ_i}g_{k_i}\). Operands may coincide, and an earlier register may be used arbitrarily many times. One register is designated as output. The program computes \(f\) if this output equals \(f\) as a formal polynomial. Define \(\tau(f)\) to be the least possible \(s\) among such programs. Every integer polynomial can be constructed in finitely many operations, so this minimum exists. When \(s=0\), only \(1\) or \(x\) can be output.

Every new arithmetic register costs one operation, including operations used to build integer constants. In particular \(2\), \(0\) and \(-1\) are not additional free inputs. There is no division, primitive exponentiation, comparison, conditional branch or access to a supplied coefficient list. The finite program may be chosen separately for each polynomial; there is no uniformity requirement on these choices. Intermediate degrees, coefficient sizes and integer magnitudes are unrestricted. Cost measures arithmetic operations, not the number of bits in coefficients, a formula without shared registers or the bit length of the program encoding.

For \(f\ne0\), define \(z_{\mathbb Z}(f)=|\{a\in\mathbb Z:f(a)=0\}|\), counting negative roots, zero and positive roots once each, regardless of multiplicity. This cardinality is finite because a nonzero univariate polynomial has at most its degree many roots; a nonzero constant has no roots. The zero polynomial is excluded. The exponent \(C\) must be one constant for all \(f\), without dependence on degree, coefficients, root sizes or the choice of an optimal program. The question asks only for a bound, not for an efficient root-counting or root-finding algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the universal bound or its logical negation, \(\forall C\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}\ \exists f\in\mathbb Z[x]\setminus\{0\}:z_{\mathbb Z}(f)>(1+\tau(f))^C\). A positive answer may use any one absolute exponent; a negative answer must exclude all such exponents. No computable rule for choosing the counterexample polynomials is required. A counterexample to just one proposed exponent, bounds for a restricted program class, multiplicity counts, or results only about real or complex roots do not settle this full target. Conditional consequences of the conjecture are not proofs of it.
cards.why: The conjecture asks whether a polynomial compressed into a short arithmetic computation can nevertheless have very many distinct integer zeros. Its elementary statement links arithmetic structure to fundamental lower bounds in algebraic computation. A proof would imply separation of polynomial-time nondeterministic and deterministic computation over the complex numbers, as well as important constant-free circuit separations; neither consequence is presently supplied by the conjecture itself.

importance.reason: A central arithmetic complexity conjecture with a very elementary statement and strong consequences for algebraic P versus NP and constant-free circuit lower bounds.

progress.text: Shub and Smale connect the complexity of integer computations to infeasibility testing over the complex numbers. Smale’s later Problem 4 explicitly records the distinct-integer-root conjecture and its complex P versus NP consequence.

The SIAM paper on semialgebraic proofs publishes conditional IPS lower bounds from the root conjecture over rational functions and from a distinct factorial-multiple hypothesis over the rationals.
A Zenodo preprint reports a finite census through eight operations with free constants -1,0,1. Its computation is unverified here and its finite scope does not resolve a universal exponent.

A bounded later-work check through 14 September 2026 found no proof or refutation of this exact statement. context_blocks.text: After \(s\) squarings, the program for \(x^{2^s}\) has only \(s\) operations but exponential degree. In general \(\deg f\leq2^{\tau(f)}\), giving only \(z_{\mathbb Z}(f)\leq2^{\tau(f)}\). The example has just one distinct integer root, although that root has multiplicity \(2^s\). This is why both the arithmetic compression and the word “distinct” matter.

The corresponding unrestricted real-root assertion is false. Let \(q_0(x)=x\) and \(q_{j+1}(x)=q_j(x)^2-2\). Building 2 once and using two operations per iteration gives \(\tau(q_j)\leq2j+1\). The identity \(q_j(2\cos\theta)=2\cos(2^j\theta)\) shows that \(q_j\) has \(2^j\) distinct real roots. Integer roots impose a substantially different constraint.

Smale’s Problem 4 records the root-count question, and Rojas gives exactly the \((1+\tau)^C\) convention used here. Allowing the fixed constants \(-1,0,1\) for free changes operation counts by at most two relative to the present convention; it does not change whether some polynomial root bound exists. Exact small-length records do depend on the convention. Arbitrary free integer constants constitute a different cost model.

Shub and Smale’s work connects short integer computations with feasibility of polynomial systems over \(\mathbb C\). Smale’s later Problem 4 explicitly states that the root conjecture implies \(\mathrm P_{\mathbb C}\ne\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb C}\) in the Blum–Shub–Smale model. This model has exact complex arithmetic and equality tests at unit cost. The implication is about that algebraic model; it does not itself assert Boolean \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

Rojas’s Theorem 1 proves that a polynomial bound just for integer roots congruent to 1 modulo one fixed prime already implies the full conjecture. His Theorem 3 gives a bound \(\exp(O(s\log(s+1)))\) on rational roots in terms of additive complexity \(s\), a measure charging additions while allowing powers and multiplicative expressions more freely. This does not give a polynomial bound in the full operation count \(\tau\).

Alekseev, Grigoriev, Hirsch and Tzameret record the implication \(\mathrm{VP}^0\ne\mathrm{VNP}^0\) for constant-free algebraic complexity, and obtain conditional lower bounds in the Ideal Proof System for a binary-value variant over rational functions. Their separate hypothesis about nonzero multiples of factorials yields a different lower bound over the rationals. These hypotheses and coefficient domains are distinct, and the results do not directly give Frege lower bounds for Boolean formulas.

Santibañez-Leal’s Zenodo preprint, version 0.03 dated 20 August 2026, reports an exhaustive census through eight operations using free constants \(-1,0,1\). The computation has not been independently reproduced for this card. A finite census, even if correct, does not establish or refute a bound with one exponent for every program length.

cards.context:
After \(s\) squarings, the program for \(x^{2^s}\) has only \(s\) operations but exponential degree. In general \(\deg f\leq2^{\tau(f)}\), giving only \(z_{\mathbb Z}(f)\leq2^{\tau(f)}\). The example has just one distinct integer root, although that root has multiplicity \(2^s\). This is why both the arithmetic compression and the word “distinct” matter.

The corresponding unrestricted real-root assertion is false. Let \(q_0(x)=x\) and \(q_{j+1}(x)=q_j(x)^2-2\). Building 2 once and using two operations per iteration gives \(\tau(q_j)\leq2j+1\). The identity \(q_j(2\cos\theta)=2\cos(2^j\theta)\) shows that \(q_j\) has \(2^j\) distinct real roots. Integer roots impose a substantially different constraint.

Smale’s Problem 4 records the root-count question, and Rojas gives exactly the \((1+\tau)^C\) convention used here. Allowing the fixed constants \(-1,0,1\) for free changes operation counts by at most two relative to the present convention; it does not change whether some polynomial root bound exists. Exact small-length records do depend on the convention. Arbitrary free integer constants constitute a different cost model.

Shub and Smale’s work connects short integer computations with feasibility of polynomial systems over \(\mathbb C\). Smale’s later Problem 4 explicitly states that the root conjecture implies \(\mathrm P_{\mathbb C}\ne\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb C}\) in the Blum–Shub–Smale model. This model has exact complex arithmetic and equality tests at unit cost. The implication is about that algebraic model; it does not itself assert Boolean \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

Rojas’s Theorem 1 proves that a polynomial bound just for integer roots congruent to 1 modulo one fixed prime already implies the full conjecture. His Theorem 3 gives a bound \(\exp(O(s\log(s+1)))\) on rational roots in terms of additive complexity \(s\), a measure charging additions while allowing powers and multiplicative expressions more freely. This does not give a polynomial bound in the full operation count \(\tau\).

Alekseev, Grigoriev, Hirsch and Tzameret record the implication \(\mathrm{VP}^0\ne\mathrm{VNP}^0\) for constant-free algebraic complexity, and obtain conditional lower bounds in the Ideal Proof System for a binary-value variant over rational functions. Their separate hypothesis about nonzero multiples of factorials yields a different lower bound over the rationals. These hypotheses and coefficient domains are distinct, and the results do not directly give Frege lower bounds for Boolean formulas.

Santibañez-Leal’s Zenodo preprint, version 0.03 dated 20 August 2026, reports an exhaustive census through eight operations using free constants \(-1,0,1\). The computation has not been independently reproduced for this card. A finite census, even if correct, does not establish or refute a bound with one exponent for every program length.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
